title: Schema
description: Define the shape of your data
section: Define the shape of your data
content: A schema describes the collections, their fields, indexes, and relations.

title: Schema
description: Define the shape of your data
content:
Use defineSchema() with createDatabase() to keep the schema's literal field
types and infer collection records:



defineSchema() preserves TypeScript literal types. Collection names that
match the schema are inferred, but the library also has a general string
overload, so undeclared names are not guaranteed to be rejected by TypeScript.
They are still checked at runtime when a schema is configured. Do not rely on
schema construction to validate every relation target or unknown field-type
string; cover those definitions in application tests.

title: Schema
description: Define the shape of your data
content:
version must be a positive integer. collections should include
the collections the application uses. IndexedDB uses the version to trigger
object-store and index upgrades.

title: Schema
description: Define the shape of your data
content:
| Option | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| type | "string" \| "number" \| "boolean" \| "object" \| "array" | Data type |
| required | boolean | Throw if missing |
| default | unknown or () => unknown | Applied when omitted or undefined; null is not replaced |
| min | number | Minimum value (number fields) |
| max | number | Maximum value (number fields) |
| maxLength | number | Max string length |
| items | FieldDefinition | Schema for array items |
| unique | boolean | Enforce uniqueness via index |
| validate | "email" \| "url" \| RegExp | Built-in validators (string fields) |

title: Schema
description: Define the shape of your data
content:
Indexes can accelerate matching a single field for ==, >, =, and
<=. The query planner chooses at most one suitable scalar index and applies
remaining predicates as filters; compound-index planning is not supported.
Unique indexes reject duplicate values at the storage layer.

title: Schema
description: Define the shape of your data
content:
Lazy relation getters and eager loading are built into the core — no plugin is
required. Relation declarations do not enforce foreign-key integrity, and
schema setup does not verify that relation targets exist.

title: Schema
description: Define the shape of your data
content:
Core validation runs without the validation plugin and covers:Required fieldsType checking (including array item types)String max lengthNumber min/maxEmail and URL format and regular-expression patternsUnknown field rejection

The validationPlugin() adds extra built-in and custom rules; it is not
required for the schema rules above. Defaults are applied during writes, not
retroactively to existing records.

title: Collection
description: Read and write records
content: A Collection maps to a single table or object store. All operations are async.

title: Collection
description: Read and write records
content:
Generates a UUID (crypto.randomUUID() or fallback) if no id is providedApplies schema defaultsValidates against schemaRuns onBeforeCreate plugin hooks (can modify data)Creates record in adapterRuns onAfterCreate plugin hooksEmits a change event

Generated IDs are strings. You may instead provide a string or numeric ID.
Duplicate IDs and unique-index violations currently reject with a plain
Error, not a dedicated duplicate-record error class.

title: Collection
description: Read and write records
content:
get returns a single record or undefined. getAll returns every record.



createMany(data) creates multiple records. The built-in IndexedDB and memory
adapters perform it atomically; custom adapters without a native bulk-create
implementation use sequential creates and may leave earlier records written if
a later create fails.

title: Collection
description: Read and write records
content: Merges changes with existing dataValidates the merged resultRuns onBeforeUpdate / onAfterUpdate plugin hooksThrows if the record does not existEmits a change event

title: Collection
description: Read and write records
content: Runs onBeforeDelete / onAfterDelete plugin hooksEmits a change event for each deleted recorddelete is a no-op if the record does not exist (a change event may still be emitted)deleteMany skips missing IDs

title: Collection
description: Read and write records
content: If data.id matches an existing record, updates it. Otherwise creates it.

title: Model
description: The record wrapper with methods and relation getters
section: The record wrapper with methods and relation getters
content:
Every record returned from a collection is wrapped in a Model proxy.
You can access fields directly — no .get("field") calls needed.

title: Model
description: The record wrapper with methods and relation getters
content:
The model is a Proxy that forwards property access to the underlying data.
Direct writes are rejected; use .update() to persist changes.

title: Model

title: Model
description: The record wrapper with methods and relation getters
content:
When the schema defines relations, the model auto-attaches lazy relation getters
(no plugin required):



Each relation getter returns a QueryBuilder pre-filtered to match the
relation. A belongs_to getter is a query builder too, so use .first() to
load the referenced model. Relation access does not check referential integrity.

Use load() when you want the resolved related model or array directly rather
than a query builder:



load("belongsTo" | "hasOne") resolves to one model or undefined;
load("hasMany") resolves to an array of models.

title: Query Engine
description: Filter, sort, and paginate records
content:
QueryBuilder provides a fluent API for reading data. It does not support joins;
use relations for related data.

title: Query Engine
description: Filter, sort, and paginate records
content: Supported operators: ==, !=, >, =, <=

title: Query Engine
description: Filter, sort, and paginate records
content: Groups conditions with OR logic. Each orWhere block is one group.

title: Query Engine
description: Filter, sort, and paginate records
content: Only one sort field per query. Passing multiple entries picks the first.

title: Query Engine
description: Filter, sort, and paginate records
content: Use offset with limit for pagination. Offset skips records before slicing.

title: Query Engine
description: Filter, sort, and paginate records
content:
Case-insensitive substring search (String.includes()) over the selected
field. This works without a plugin and scans candidate records.

title: Query Engine
description: Filter, sort, and paginate records
content:
match() tokenizes the input, removes common English stop words, and requires
all remaining whole-word tokens to match. By default it searches the
collection's schema searchable fields. Unlike search(), it is not a
substring query.

The FTS plugin can accelerate matching with
an inverted index; it is optional for correct search results.

title: Query Engine
description: Filter, sort, and paginate records
content: first() is equivalent to .limit(1).fetch() then returning results[0].

title: Query Engine
description: Filter, sort, and paginate records
content:
The QueryPlanner examines conditions and indexes to pick a strategy:

| Strategy | When | How |
|----------|------|-----|
| idlookup | Querying by id field with == | Direct adapter lookup |
| indexscan | A suitable single-field index exists | Uses the best available index, then filters remaining conditions |
| full_scan | No index match | Iterates all records, filters in memory |

Sorting is applied in memory. The default order is ascending by primary key.
Only one sort field is used (the first supplied); offset and limit are applied
after filtering. Cursor pagination and compound indexes are not supported.

title: Query Engine
description: Filter, sort, and paginate records
content:
Uses JavaScript's  comparison. Numbers sort numerically and strings
lexicographically; avoid mixing incomparable field types.

title: Transactions
description: Atomic operations with automatic rollback
content:
Transactions group multiple database operations into one atomic unit. If the
callback throws, the adapter rolls back its writes.

title: Transactions
description: Atomic operations with automatic rollback
content:
Both creates succeed together, or neither is committed. Transactional writes
run validation and before-hooks in the transaction; after-hooks and change
events run only after commit. Aborted writes emit no post-commit events.

title: Transactions
description: Atomic operations with automatic rollback
content:
Inside a transaction callback, use the transaction-scoped collection returned
by ctx.collection(name). Do not use db.collection() for work that must
participate in the transaction.

| Method | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| findAll | () => Promise | All records in the collection |
| findById | (id: ID) => Promise | Single record by ID |
| create | (data: Partial) => Promise | Create a new record |
| update | (id: ID, changes: Partial) => Promise | Update an existing record |
| delete | (id: ID) => Promise | Delete a record |

The transaction-scoped collection provides CRUD operations; it is not the full
query-builder API. Keep reads and writes inside the callback on that scoped
collection.

title: Transactions
description: Atomic operations with automatic rollback
content: If the callback throws, all changes are discarded:

title: Transactions
description: Atomic operations with automatic rollback
content:
Transactions return whatever the callback returns:



The IndexedDB adapter uses a native IndexedDB transaction. IndexedDB may
automatically close a transaction while the callback awaits unrelated work
(such as a network request or timer), so perform external work before or after
the transaction. The memory adapter uses an in-memory snapshot; its data is
still volatile and is lost on disconnect.

Avoid nested transactions. Keep the callback limited to its scoped database
operations so all reads and writes share the same transaction.

title: Error Handling
description: Working with ctrodb's error classes
content:
ctrodb exports typed errors for connection, schema, validation, and storage
failures. Duplicate-ID and unique-index violations currently reject with a
plain Error, not a dedicated duplicate error class.

title: Error Handling
description: Working with ctrodb's error classes
content:
QueryError is also exported, but is not used for ordinary built-in
query failures. RecordNotFoundError is thrown when updating a missing
record. Deleting a missing ID is a no-op.

title: Error Handling
description: Working with ctrodb's error classes
content:
Thrown when using a collection before the database is connected.



Can also include a custom reason passed to the constructor.

title: Error Handling
description: Working with ctrodb's error classes
content: Thrown when the schema configuration is invalid.

title: Error Handling
description: Working with ctrodb's error classes
content: Thrown when a record violates schema validation rules. Contains field, collection, and value properties for detailed error handling.

title: Error Handling
description: Working with ctrodb's error classes
content:
CollectionNotFoundError(name, availableCollections?) — when requesting an undeclared collection from a schema-constrained databaseRecordNotFoundError(collection, id) — when updating a missing recordStorageQuotaError(message) — for storage quota failuresQueryError(message) — exported, but not used for ordinary built-in query failures

You can use them in your own code or plugins for consistent error types.

title: Error Handling
description: Working with ctrodb's error classes
content:
logLevel is accepted in DatabaseConfig and reserved for future use:



| Level | Intended behavior (not yet implemented) |
|-------|-----------------------------------------|
| "debug" | All internal operations logged |
| "info" | Major lifecycle events (connect, disconnect) |
| "warn" | Recoverable issues (blocked IDB) |
| "error" | Failures and exceptions |
| "silent" | No logging |

title: Adapters Overview
description: Storage backends — persistence, lifecycle, and how to choose
section: Storage backends — persistence, lifecycle, and how to choose
content:
Adapters are the persistence layer of ctrodb. They handle all read and write
operations to the underlying storage. The rest of the library (schema
validation, query engine, reactivity, plugins) is adapter-agnostic — swap the
adapter and everything still works.

title: Adapters Overview
description: Storage backends — persistence, lifecycle, and how to choose
content:
| Adapter | Environment | Persistence |
|---|---|---|
| IndexedDBAdapter | Browser (all modern) | Persists in IndexedDB — survives reloads and tab closures |
| MemoryAdapter | Node.js, browser, Deno | In-memory Map — lost on process exit or page reload |

title: Adapters Overview
description: Storage backends — persistence, lifecycle, and how to choose
content:
When no adapter is specified, ctrodb selects one automatically. The runtime
checks for window.indexedDB; environments without it use memory storage.



The detection checks for window.indexedDB at runtime:

title: Adapters Overview
description: Storage backends — persistence, lifecycle, and how to choose
content: You can pick an adapter explicitly using the adapter config option:

title: Adapters Overview
description: Storage backends — persistence, lifecycle, and how to choose
content:
Every adapter follows the same lifecycle:





The Database class manages this lifecycle automatically — you don't call
connect() or disconnect() on the adapter directly. Memory data is cleared
on disconnect, so it is not suitable for persistence.

title: Adapters Overview
description: Storage backends — persistence, lifecycle, and how to choose
content:
Every adapter implements the StorageAdapter interface:



createMany, findByIds, count, and hasIndex are optional capabilities.
When createMany is absent, ctrodb falls back to sequential creates, which
cannot guarantee all-or-nothing behavior. The QueryRange passed to
scanIndex() is storage-neutral and does not require the browser's
IDBKeyRange.

title: Adapters Overview
description: Storage backends — persistence, lifecycle, and how to choose
content:
IDs are UUID strings generated by the Collection layer:



Adapters themselves do not generate IDs — they receive the full record with
id already set. If you call an adapter's create() directly without an id,
some adapters (like MemoryAdapter) will throw.

You can supply your own IDs:

title: Adapters Overview
description: Storage backends — persistence, lifecycle, and how to choose
content:
Adapters receive the full schema configuration during connect(), which
includes:



The IndexedDBAdapter uses this to create object stores and indexes during
version upgrades. Define the collections in your schema before connecting;
the memory adapter pre-creates collection maps.

title: Adapters Overview
description: Storage backends — persistence, lifecycle, and how to choose
content:
All adapters support transactions. If the transaction callback throws, all
changes are rolled back.

ctx.collection(name) returns a collection scoped to the current transaction.
Use it for all reads and writes that must be atomic:



Do not use regular database collections or perform unrelated asynchronous
work inside the callback. IndexedDB may automatically close a transaction
while it is waiting on unrelated promises.

title: Adapters Overview
description: Storage backends — persistence, lifecycle, and how to choose
content:
Adapters implement scanIndex() for indexed lookups by field value. This
powers the query planner's indexscan strategy and internal indexed queries.

IndexedDBAdapter: Uses native IDB indexes — fast, only returns matching
records.

MemoryAdapter**: Does a full collection scan with in-memory range and
post-filter matching.

title: Adapters Overview
description: Storage backends — persistence, lifecycle, and how to choose
content:
Both adapters implement a key-value metadata store for internal state:



The IndexedDBAdapter stores metadata in a special ctrodbmeta object store.
The MemoryAdapter stores it in a private Map.

title: Adapters Overview
description: Storage backends — persistence, lifecycle, and how to choose
content:
Any object that satisfies the StorageAdapter interface can serve as a ctrodb
backend. See the Custom Adapters guide.

title: MemoryAdapter
description: In-memory storage for Node.js, testing, and prototyping
section: In-memory storage for Node.js, testing, and prototyping
content:
MemoryAdapter stores all data in JavaScript Map objects. Data is cleared
when the database disconnects and is lost when the process exits or page
reloads. It is the default adapter when window.indexedDB is unavailable.

title: MemoryAdapter
description: In-memory storage for Node.js, testing, and prototyping
content:
Each collection is a Map — one map per collection nameA separate Map holds metadata (schema version, etc.)On connect(), collection maps are pre-created for every entry in
  schema.collectionsIDs are not auto-generated — the adapter requires an id field on every
  record. The Collection layer always provides one (via crypto.randomUUID())Records are stored as-is but findAll() and findById() return shallow
  copies to prevent external mutation

title: MemoryAdapter
description: In-memory storage for Node.js, testing, and prototyping
content: Unit and integration testsServer-side rendering (SSR) and server componentsCLI tools and scriptsDemos and prototypingNode.js environments without IndexedDBCI pipelines (no browser required)

title: MemoryAdapter
description: In-memory storage for Node.js, testing, and prototyping
content:
The MemoryAdapter.create() method requires an id field. If you call it
directly without one, it throws:



When using Collection.create(), the Collection layer generates a UUID via
crypto.randomUUID() and passes it to the adapter — you never need to worry
about IDs in normal usage.

title: MemoryAdapter
description: In-memory storage for Node.js, testing, and prototyping
content:
The MemoryAdapter does a full collection scan and applies range and post-filter
conditions in JavaScript:



This works correctly for all query types but is O(n) — every record in the
collection is checked. For small datasets (testing, prototyping) this is fine.

title: MemoryAdapter
description: In-memory storage for Node.js, testing, and prototyping
content:
Transactions use a snapshot-and-restore mechanism:On transaction(fn) start, the adapter deep-clones all collection mapsThe callback runs against the live dataIf the callback succeeds, the snapshot is discardedIf the callback throws, the snapshot is restored — all changes are rolled
   backNested transactions are not supported



The transaction context exposes transaction-scoped collections, like the
IndexedDB adapter. Use those scoped collections inside the callback.

title: MemoryAdapter
description: In-memory storage for Node.js, testing, and prototyping
content:
Data does not persist across restartsNo concurrent access protection (single-process only)O(n) scanIndex — not suitable for large datasetsAuto-created collections (via #ensureCollection) do not apply schema
  defaults or validation — use the Collection layer for that

title: IndexedDBAdapter
description: Persistent browser storage — survives reloads and tab closures
section: Persistent browser storage — survives reloads and tab closures
content:
IndexedDBAdapter uses the browser's native IndexedDB API for persistent
storage. Data survives page reloads, tab closures, and browser restarts. It is
the default adapter in browser environments.

title: IndexedDBAdapter
description: Persistent browser storage — survives reloads and tab closures
content:
Each collection is an object store with id as the key pathSchema-defined indexes are created as native IDB indexes on each storePlugin stores (ctrodbsyncchanges, etc.) are created with id key path
  and can declare their own indexes via PluginStoreConfigA special ctrodb_meta object store holds schema version, sync state,
  and other internal metadataThe database version is driven by schema.version — bumping it triggers
  the onupgradeneeded migration handler

title: IndexedDBAdapter
description: Persistent browser storage — survives reloads and tab closures
content:
When you increase schema.version, IndexedDB fires onupgradeneeded. The
adapter creates missing object stores and indexes. Existing records are
preserved; ctrodb does not run a user-provided data-migration callback.

title: IndexedDBAdapter
description: Persistent browser storage — survives reloads and tab closures
content:
For each collection in schema.collections:If the object store doesn't exist, it is created with { keyPath: "id" }Schema-defined indexes are created: store.createIndex(field, field, { unique })

For plugin stores (schema.pluginStoreNames):If the store doesn't exist, it is created with { keyPath: "id" }If the entry is a PluginStoreConfig with indexes, those indexes are created

The ctrodbmeta store is created if it doesn't exist.

Removed collections are not automatically deleted, and removed or changed
fields are not migrated. Schema versioning creates missing stores/indexes but
does not transform existing records. Plan any data backfill as an explicit
application migration.

title: IndexedDBAdapter
description: Persistent browser storage — survives reloads and tab closures
content:
Unlike the MemoryAdapter (which scans in JavaScript), the IndexedDBAdapter uses
native IDB indexes for scanIndex(). The public adapter contract passes a
storage-neutral QueryRange; the adapter translates it into an IndexedDB
range internally:



This means:Only records matching the index range are loaded from disk — not the
  full collectionThe native index avoids scanning the full collection when the range is selectiveRemaining conditions are applied after the index lookup

title: IndexedDBAdapter
description: Persistent browser storage — survives reloads and tab closures
content:
QueryRange contains optional lower / upper scalar values and
lowerOpen / upperOpen flags. An IndexedDB adapter can convert this
descriptor into native IDBKeyRange values:

title: IndexedDBAdapter
description: Persistent browser storage — survives reloads and tab closures
content:
The adapter must honor the supplied post-filter conditions. The query executor
also evaluates query predicates against candidates. .search() remains a
substring scan; match() may use FTS-index candidates, but still verifies
matching results.

title: IndexedDBAdapter
description: Persistent browser storage — survives reloads and tab closures
content:
Transactions use a native IndexedDB transaction. Reads and writes made
through the transaction-scoped collections share its transaction.



The transaction context returns a bound collection proxy — you call
methods without passing the collection name:



Keep the callback free of unrelated asynchronous work: IndexedDB can
automatically close a transaction when it is idle, including while awaiting
network requests or timers.

title: IndexedDBAdapter
description: Persistent browser storage — survives reloads and tab closures
content:
If the transaction callback throws, tx.abort() is called — IndexedDB
automatically discards all writes in the transaction scope.

title: IndexedDBAdapter
description: Persistent browser storage — survives reloads and tab closures
content:
Metadata is stored in the ctrodbmeta object store:



This store is used internally for schema version tracking and by the sync
engine for cursor state (sync:lastPullCursor, sync:lastSyncAt).

title: IndexedDBAdapter
description: Persistent browser storage — survives reloads and tab closures
content:
Plugins that declare storeNames with PluginStoreConfig get their indexes
created during migration:



These indexes are created during onupgradeneeded when the store is first
created, exactly like schema-defined collection indexes.

title: IndexedDBAdapter
description: Persistent browser storage — survives reloads and tab closures
content:
deleteMany() uses a single readwrite transaction and iterates through the
provided IDs — each delete is an individual IDBRequest within the same
transaction scope:

title: IndexedDBAdapter
description: Persistent browser storage — survives reloads and tab closures
content:
Not available in Node.js without fake-indexeddb polyfillSize limits vary by browser (typically 50 MB to unlimited for most
  modern browsers). Chrome asks the user for permission above a threshold.Blocked on version change — if another tab has the same database open
  with an older version, the onupgradeneeded event fires but the upgrade
  is blocked until all other tabs close. The adapter logs a warning when this
  happens.No support for modifying existing indexes — to change an index, you must
  create a new store or delete and recreate the database.

title: Custom Adapters
description: Implementing a storage backend for ctrodb
section: Implementing a storage backend for ctrodb
content:
Pass an object implementing StorageAdapter to Database when you need
storage beyond the built-in IndexedDB and memory adapters. The adapter handles
storage only; Collection remains responsible for model wrapping, schema
defaults, validation, plugin hooks, and change events.

title: Custom Adapters
description: Implementing a storage backend for ctrodb
content:
createMany, findByIds, count, and hasIndex are optional adapter
capabilities. If createMany is absent, ctrodb creates the records
sequentially; that fallback is not atomic. If hasIndex is absent, the query
planner treats the adapter as having no native indexes.

QueryRange is storage-neutral. It contains optional lower and upper
values plus lowerOpen and upperOpen flags; do not require browser

title: Custom Adapters
description: Implementing a storage backend for ctrodb
content:
TransactionContext.collection(name) returns a scoped CRUD handle. Every
operation through that handle must participate in the same transaction:



The scoped handle provides create, findById, findAll, update, and
delete. It is not the regular Collection API and does not provide query
builders. A custom adapter's transaction implementation must roll back all
writes when the callback throws and resolve only after commit.

For browser storage, avoid awaiting unrelated work such as network calls or
timers inside the callback: native IndexedDB transactions may close while
idle. Perform that work before or after the transaction.

title: Custom Adapters
description: Implementing a storage backend for ctrodb
content:
Implement scanIndex() using the supplied scalar range and then apply every
where condition in postFilters. QueryCondition may also contain
search or match predicates; do not silently treat an unsupported predicate
as satisfied. The query executor applies predicates to returned candidates,
so an indexed scan may return a superset but must not omit matching records.

If implementing createMany(), validate the entire batch for adapter-level
constraints before writing and commit all records atomically. The collection
layer validates schema rules before invoking the adapter.

title: Plugin Overview
description: Extend ctrodb with lifecycle hooks
content:
Plugins hook into database and collection lifecycle events. Core schema
validation and the built-in relation APIs work without their corresponding
plugins; those plugins add optional capabilities rather than enabling core
behavior.

title: Plugin Overview
description: Extend ctrodb with lifecycle hooks
content:
Hooks may be asynchronous; ctrodb awaits them. Before-hooks run before a write
and may transform data. After-hook failures are logged and do not roll back a
write that has already been committed.

onDatabaseDestroy() runs when db.disconnect() is called. Hook contexts
include origin: "local" | "remote"; the sync engine uses "remote" for
incoming writes. For createMany(), a plugin implementing
onAfterCreateMany() receives the batch once instead of receiving an
onAfterCreate() call for every record.

For update():onBeforeUpdate — plugins can modify changesSchema validation (merged with existing)Adapter updates recordonAfterUpdate — after the write succeeds

For delete():onBeforeDeleteAdapter deletes recordonAfterDelete — after the write succeeds

title: Sync Overview
description: Offline-first synchronization for ctrodb
content:
The sync plugin tracks local collection changes, pushes them to a remote
transport, pulls remote changes, and resolves push conflicts. Local writes are
available before synchronization completes. The engine retries eligible
failures with exponential backoff; use IndexedDB when the queue must survive
browser reloads because memory storage is volatile.

title: Sync Overview
description: Offline-first synchronization for ctrodb
content:
| Concept | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| ChangeTracker | Records every create/update/delete to ctrodbsyncchanges store |
| SyncEngine | Orchestrates push → resolve conflicts → pull cycle |
| Transport | Sends changes to / receives changes from a remote server |
| ConflictResolver | Determines which version wins when local and remote disagree |
| SYNCSTORE | Internal IndexedDB store (ctrodbsync_changes) with status and timestamp indexes |

title: Sync Overview
description: Offline-first synchronization for ctrodb
content: A single sync cycle runs:Push — sends pending & failed local changes to the serverResolve conflicts — applies conflict strategy to any push conflictsPull — fetches remote changes since last cursorCleanup — removes committed records from the sync queue

title: Sync Overview
description: Offline-first synchronization for ctrodb
content: Each tracked change moves through these states:pending — waiting to be pushedsyncing — currently being transmittedcommitted — successfully pushed (removed on next successful sync)failed — push failed, will be retried

and the local-change debounce is 500 milliseconds. The default push and pull

per change; exhausted entries remain failed until manually retried. The
collections option filters both push and pull. Queue records move through

with the sync utilities.

cursor. Pagination continues until the server indicates that no more changes
are available. A safety limit of 1,000 pages stops a pull if the server never
finishes pagination.

and cap at five minutes. Each delay uses 75%-125% jitter. After 50 consecutive
failed sync cycles, automatic retries stop scheduling; applications can
surface the error and request a manual sync.

When the same record is modified on two devices before either change reaches
the server, a conflict occurs. ConflictResolverEngine determines which
version wins.

title: Conflict Resolution
description: Strategies for handling conflicting changes
content:
Set via the strategy option in SyncPluginConfig:



| Strategy | Behavior |
|----------|----------|
| "lww" (default) | Last-writer-wins. Compares timestamps; remote wins ties. |
| "client-wins" | Local version always wins. Server is overwritten. |
| "server-wins" | Remote version always wins. Local changes are discarded. |
| "custom" | Your own logic via conflictResolver function. |

description: Strategies for handling conflicting changes
content: The default strategy. Compares localTimestamp and remoteTimestamp:If local is newer → local winsIf remote is newer → remote winsIf timestamps are equal → remote wins (tiebreaker)

Local changes always overwrite the server. Use this when the client is the
authoritative source (e.g., a note-taking app where the client is always

Remote changes always overwrite local data. Use this when the server is
the single source of truth (e.g., collaborative editing with a central
authority).

description: Strategies for handling conflicting changes
content:
"local" — the sync engine marks the change as committed; server state is ignored"remote" — the sync engine applies the remote data to the local store"merged" — the sync engine writes your merged payload to the store

For "remote" and "merged", the engine handles all CRUD cases:

| Local exists | Remote data | Action |
|-------------|-------------|--------|
| Yes | Non-null | Update local record |
| No | Non-null | Create local record |
| Yes | Null | Delete local record |
| No | Null | No-op |

title: Production Patterns
description: Deploying and scaling the sync engine
content:
The sync engine is designed for offline-first applications:All writes are local first — the library writes to IndexedDB immediately,
   sync happens asynchronouslyQueue persists across sessions — pending changes survive page reloads,
   tab closures, and browser crashes (via init() crash recovery)Background sync — auto-sync interval keeps data fresh without user
   interactionOnline recovery — when the browser comes online, sync triggers
   automatically

title: Production Patterns
description: Deploying and scaling the sync engine

sync queue. When BroadcastChannel is available, a local change notifies
other tabs and triggers a debounced sync. The server should still handle
repeated requests idempotently.

description: Deploying and scaling the sync engine
content: Your server should:Accept POST /push with { changes: SyncChangeRecord[] }Apply each change to the authoritative databaseDetect conflicts (same record modified since last sync) and return themReturn { accepted, conflicts, errors }

content:
Pass authentication via headers in the transport config:



The sync engine does not manage auth — pass the HTTP token from your app's
auth flow. For WsTransport, configured headers are sent in an auth protocol
message after connection; they are not browser WebSocket handshake headers.
After refreshing an expired token, retry queued failures using the sync API or
queue tools.

title: Production Patterns
description: Deploying and scaling the sync engine
content:
Push batch size — tune pushBatchSize based on your average record
  size and server capacity. Smaller batches reduce per-request payload but
  increase request count.Pull batch size — larger pullBatchSize reduces round-trips but
  increases per-response payload. Default 100 is good for most apps.Sync interval — intervalMs of 30s balances freshness with battery
  and bandwidth. For real-time apps, use WsTransport instead.Debounce — debounceMs of 500-1000ms coalesces rapid local writes
  into a single sync request.Response validation — validatePushResult and validatePullResult
  validate server responses. Treat malformed responses as a protocol error
  and correct the server contract rather than disabling validation.

title: Upgrading to ctrodb 1.13.2
description: Current-v1 upgrade checklist and migration notes
content:
Persistence: the automatic adapter uses IndexedDB when
  window.indexedDB exists and memory otherwise. Memory data is volatile and
  is cleared on disconnect.Relations: relation getters and eager loading are built into the core;
  relationsPlugin() is not required. Relation declarations do not enforce
  foreign-key integrity.Validation: schema validation runs without validationPlugin(). The
  plugin adds its own extra built-in and custom rules.Search: .search() is a case-insensitive substring scan. .match()
  performs tokenized AND matching over searchable fields; the FTS plugin can
  accelerate it but is not required for correct results.React: prefer  over the deprecated global
  setDefaultDatabase() and getDb() helpers, which are planned for removal
  in v2.

title: Upgrading to ctrodb 1.13.2
description: Current-v1 upgrade checklist and migration notes
content:
For IndexedDB, increment schema.version when stores or indexes need an
upgrade. ctrodb creates missing object stores and indexes but does not provide
a user migration callback, transform existing records, or delete stores that
were removed from the schema. Backfill or transform records with an explicit
application migration, and test it against a copy of representative data.

Defaults apply on create/update when a field is omitted or undefined; they
do not backfill existing records and do not replace null. Adding a required
field therefore needs an explicit backfill before relying on the new
constraint.

section: Lessons learned from building ctrodb — a zero-dependency client-side database
content:
Building ctrodb through six alpha releases to a stable v1.0.0 taught us a few things about TypeScript library design. Here is what we learned.

Historical perspective: This post describes the library as it stood at
v1.0.0. Test counts, bundle-size notes, plugin architecture, and plans below
are from that release; the current documented release is v1.13.2. See the
current upgrade guide for current behavior.
author: ctrodb team

title: From Alpha to v1.0.0: Building a TypeScript Library
description: Lessons learned from building ctrodb — a zero-dependency client-side database
content:
The decision to have zero runtime dependencies shaped the entire architecture. Every feature had to be implemented from scratch or not included. This forced us to:Write our own reactive signal implementation (35 lines)Build a custom query planner instead of using a libraryKeep the bundle small (~25 KB gzip)

Users appreciate not having to audit a deep dependency tree.
author: ctrodb team

title: From Alpha to v1.0.0: Building a TypeScript Library
description: Lessons learned from building ctrodb — a zero-dependency client-side database
content:
Exporting proper types is more valuable than writing separate docs for every interface. The SchemaConfig type tells you exactly what a schema looks like. The StorageAdapter interface shows every method an adapter needs.

We export all public types alongside the classes. Users get autocomplete and type checking without switching between docs and code.
author: ctrodb team

title: From Alpha to v1.0.0: Building a TypeScript Library
description: Lessons learned from building ctrodb — a zero-dependency client-side database
content:
The test suite grew from 30 tests in alpha.1 to 190 tests in v1.0.0. Every bug fix started with a failing test. The test coverage includes:Schema validation edge casesAll query operators with various data typesAdapter-specific behaviorPlugin hook execution orderReact hook rendering cycles

Integration tests catch issues that unit tests miss. A test that creates, queries, updates, and deletes records in sequence reveals timing and state management bugs.
author: ctrodb team

title: From Alpha to v1.0.0: Building a TypeScript Library
description: Lessons learned from building ctrodb — a zero-dependency client-side database
content:
At v1.0.0, FTS, relations, and validation were presented as plugins. In the
current v1.13.2 release, schema validation and relation APIs also work without
their corresponding plugins; the FTS plugin remains an optional index for
tokenized match() queries. The plugin hook interface has evolved since this
post, including async lifecycle hooks and write context.
author: ctrodb team

title: From Alpha to v1.0.0: Building a TypeScript Library
description: Lessons learned from building ctrodb — a zero-dependency client-side database
content:
We went from alpha.1 to alpha.6, then straight to v1.0.0. The jump to stable was possible because:The API surface settled after alpha.3Internal refactors did not change public typesTest coverage gave confidence

One thing we would do differently: ship the React bindings earlier.

collection callback parameters are typed as unknown in the public interface.

title: Why Client-Side Databases Matter
description: The shift towards local-first applications and what it means for developers
content:
Users expect instant feedback. A local database avoids waiting for a network
round trip, although its reads and writes are still asynchronous operations.
Remote requests add variable latency, and that adds up.
author: ctrodb team

title: Why Client-Side Databases Matter
description: The shift towards local-first applications and what it means for developers
content: Mobile users go through tunnels. Desktop users lose WiFi. Progressive web apps need to work without a connection. A client-side database means your app keeps running when the network drops, and syncs when it comes back.
author: ctrodb team

title: Why Client-Side Databases Matter
description: The shift towards local-first applications and what it means for developers
content:
Existing client-side storage options each have trade-offs:localStorage: synchronous, blocking, strings only, with browser-managed
  storage limitsIndexedDB raw: powerful but verbose, no schema, error-proneSQLite (via WASM): heavy, complex, overkill for most appsctrodb: schema-driven and reactive, with IndexedDB and memory adapters

ctrodb wraps IndexedDB and memory storage with a TypeScript API. Its automatic
adapter uses IndexedDB when available and otherwise uses volatile memory
storage. Define a schema for validation and indexes, and subscribe to changes
through its event system.
author: ctrodb team

title: Why Client-Side Databases Matter
description: The shift towards local-first applications and what it means for developers
content:
The most successful local-first apps follow a pattern:Local database is the source of truthUI renders from local data — reads avoid the network round tripWrites go to local DB first — the UI need not wait for a network round tripBackground sync pushes to a server when connected

ctrodb provides the local database and also offers an optional sync plugin with
HTTP, WebSocket, and custom transports. You still choose and operate the server
and sync protocol for your application; synchronization starts only when
configured.
author: ctrodb team

title: Why Client-Side Databases Matter
description: The shift towards local-first applications and what it means for developers
content:
If you are building a new app, start with local persistence and add remote sync
when the product needs it. You can build and use local-first features without
configuring a sync server.
